questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to live in a city which was not too big to be explored within the 4 months of my exchange. It was also important for me that the highlands of Scotland was so close, so I could go on weekend trips and hike in the beautiful nature. Furthermore, finding courses I could take at the university that would allow me to get pre-approval at KU was crucial for my choice of destination. This was of course easier in Scotland as an English speaking country, where I could follow all courses at the university.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I had a lovely exchange at University of Edinburgh (UoE). The student association at the university has a very strong presence and AMAZING facilities (honestly, they have a flipping castle in the middle of campus!). There are around 100 or more societies, with sports, music, theatre and academic related. Great place to meet lots of people :D
And the Erasmus Student Network also has a good handful of activities, where it's possible to connect with other exchange students :)

Edinburgh is a beautiful, easy and comfortable place to live and have a great exchange. 

But I must say, that the autumn semester in UoE is very short. It only lasts from 20th of September to mid December (my last exam was due 13th of Dec). Although it is nice to have the Holidays off, it was a very short time to learn the course material (13 weeks) where in the last two weeks, it was almost impossible to follow the lectures and read the course material, as the exam papers were already released an the hand in dates approaching (1st and 2nd of December for me).
I thought this was a shame, as I believe I could have learned much more from the professors and curriculum at UoE if I had had more time. Might be that it is a longer semester in the spring, and therefore more time for diving into the course material and spend time with all the lovely people you will meet on your exchange.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The Vistiting Students Office were very helpful and respond very quickly to all my emails. And they give you checklists on what documents etc you will need on arrival at the UoE. 

Although I was a bit on my own in figuring out immigration rules with Brexit and covid. Ended up not being that difficult, but I brought all the documents anyway.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
They could have been clearer on helping with covid and brexit immigration issues. The information on their webpage focus mainly on the rules for non-EU citizens. 
But I also didn't ask them directly to help me with this. They would probably have helped if I had asked, but I figured it out on my own.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I think you definitely find the best housing through network. I found a room in a flat with a friend of a friend of a friend of a friend (yes 4 links away). So if you know someone who might know someone in Edinburgh, ask them to ask around if they know someone who has a room where you can stay. This way you might find a cheaper rent and a better placement in the city, than if you look at FB groups where the competition can be harsh just before semester starts :)
So start searching for accommodation early.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
The dormitories ("on campus") are party places most of them. So if you're up for parties, music, meeting lots of people and living with ppl who just moved out from their parents (most of them), then the dorms are probably great for you. 
If you prefer to have your own place/kitchen and fewer drunken neighbors, maybe off campus (non domitories) are better for you. 
Flat-shares are great and exists all over town.
Areas of the city: Lots of students live in Newington and southside, which is right next to campus. Mayfield and Marchmont are not far, but can be expensive. Leith is a bit further away, but has a cool music scene and bars etc. 
West Edinburgh is a bit further from campus and I didn't go there too much. But stockbridge is a cool area and maybe decent to live in :)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I was very lucky with the flat I found right next to campus and very cheap :)
Not sure if I think this is a general thing one can expect to find as a student of UoE.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The registration as a visiting student was very easy. But the course registration was not that smooth.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
UoE do not tell visiting students what 3rd and 4th year (last years of bachelor) courses are available for exchange students until mid July. And the learning agreement needs to be signed by KU and UoE with the courses you're expected to take by 1st of August. This is a prerequisite for the Erasmus grant application and hence has consequences for when the grant is dispersed. This was quite stressful for me, as I couldn't do anything until UoE had released the courses available for enrollment, and then had to apply for them in their online platform, which also don't work very efficiently. If a course is full you have to keep applying for it every day and hope that a space opens up. And you can only change your courses until 1st of September. 
But lots of students do change courses in the first couple of weeks, so it's often possible to get the course you want. And I also did get the courses I wanted and needed for KU. It was just a stressful process, as I also had to hastily get new reapprovals for other UoE courses from KU.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Visiting Student office tried their best to help and answer quickly and I could go for a meeting with them. But the system is not the smartest.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the courses I wanted in the end.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get a bucket full of preapprovals before you go on the exchange. I mean 3-5 different reapprovals for each KU course you want to take at UoE. This way you will have more freedom if the courses are full and you need to change.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Two of my courses had good and challenging course material. The other one was a bit trivial, especially in the beginning.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took one 3rd year sociology course, which had amazing lectures, great curriculum and interesting class discussions. The course papers were interesting, inspiring and quite challenging. 

I took one 2nd year contemporary health issues course, which has interesting lectures and curriculum, but very poorly facilitated group discussions. The course assignments were also interesting and challenging. 

The third course was at the nursing faculty. This course was a bit trivial in the beginning, fx. a whole lecture on the fight or flight mechanism as one would explain it to 1st year high schoolers. But the course got better and more interesting after a couple of weeks. The course assignments were not very difficult, but still demanded a bit of work ofc.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Same divide between lectures and classes. But the classes were mainly discussions rather than teacher presentation or group work. Also, some classes were taught by professors, not student instructors, which was very inspiring.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Contemporary Feminist Issues
Contemporary Issues in Health and Wellbeing
Mental Health: Life Sciences and Nursing Care 2

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Contemporary Feminist Issues - This was extremely interesting and very well managed! Give it a go definitely :)

Contemporary Issues in Health and Wellbeing. I liked this course, although it was not as great managed and facilitated.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
The above amounts are by no means precise. I did try to monitor my spending once during my exchange, but honestly I didn't go to Scotland to spend my time budgetting. I went out a lot to enjoy the city and the nature, so I spent quite a bit on food and weekend trips.
But I had to fill in the above, so you can disregard most of it, although my rent really was 3250 kr, which is very cheap for Edinburgh! Also the travel insurance amount is correct.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
I didn't expect to pay for hiking association membership and gym membership, but I am glad I did. Also weekend trips were a tad more expensive than anticipated. But honestly, don't go with a group trip, did it once, and not worth it. Just find a group of friends, rent a car or catch a train, book an airbnb and enjoy the highlands or borderlands :)

Food was not too expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: So many societies and great facilities!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Everything you can imagine. I did hiking, choir, lindy hop, tango, blues and ceilidh dancing.
There is also a student gym (Pleasance) with equipment and classes, but you pay for your membership. They also have an indoor swimming pool.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Hiking, choir, lindy hop, tango, blues and ceilidh dancing.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to the highlands (west)! Inverness, Loch Ness, Loch Lomond, Cairngorms national park, Isle of skye etc. 
Also, heard the borderlands are nice and the cities in the east. Didn't have time to visit those.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Extremely easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Join the societies from UoE and Erasmus Student Network (ESN). Both have lots of events in the intro week.
There are not that many Scottish ppl at UoE, as this university is more expensive than the other two universities in the city. So UoE is mainly full of English ppl and exchange/foreign students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None. Just that the traffic was on the other side of the street.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The ceilidh! Scottish folk dancing - so much fun and very easy to learn. Most of the societies have a ceilidh [Kayli] dance it once or twice a year :D

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Have a LOT of preapprovals ready from KU. This means you have to look in the exchange student course finder on the UoE website a good while before the exchange starts.

2. Start looking for accommodation early and try to see if you know someone who knows someone in Edinburgh, who might be able to help.

3. Join the university societies and enjoy your time with all the other lovely students! This is also a great place to meet people with whom you can travel Scotland and visit the highlands :D

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Get a railcard if you expect to travel a lot in Scotland. Glasgow is only 50 min away by express train and worth a visit! And many more cities :)
Also
https://www.citylink.co.uk/
good place to look for traveling around.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
All the dancing communities I became a part of :D I meet amazing students from all over the world and became good friends with many of them. They will be with me even if the exchange is over :)
Also going to the highlands with my group of exchange student friends!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Having time to do all the stuff I wanted to do. Seeing the highlands, Edinburgh, other cities, studying, working, being a climate activist. Pretty packed 4 months heh..

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
Enjoy if you go! I had a great time, despite initial stress with course registration and a crammed exam period.
You'll meet great people from all over the world and have lots of amazing ppl to visit later :D

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
